To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a region of the FG responds more strongly to an entity that appears animate compared with an entity that appears inanimate, even though the entities have identical surface features; and (2) this effect is observed in a region of the fusiform gyrusthat has been previously associated with the processing of human faces.
the FG responds more strongly to animate than to inanimate agents, despite the fact that the surface features of the two agents were identical.
the FG is sensitive to animacy and that the FG is especially responsive to the faces of agents that are capable of rational goal-directed action.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what the fusiform gyrusspecialization for human faces means.
the question of whether a brain area is responding to the surface features of a face or to the more general concept of an animate agent.
the question of whether a region of the FG is specialized for processing human-like faces or whether the FG responds more generally to the presence of an animate entity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the right fusiform is sensitive to animate entities and not just human faces.
the right fusiform responds more strongly to animate than inanimate faces.
the fusiform gyrushows a bias for animate agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the FG does respond to faces, but only when those faces indicate the presence of animate agents.
the right fusiform face area is especially sensitive to whether a face-like stimulus has the capacity for goal directed actions.
the FG responds selectively to human faces when the entity is animate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FG does respond to all faces but it does not respond equally to all faces.
the FG may not respond to faces per se, but rather to the presence of human-like surface cues that are indicative of animacy.
